summary: We have developed an interactive science tool called the Lunar Landing Site Navigator. It allows us to identify good landing sites and times to land at the South Pole of the moon. Using NASA data and astronomical location and topographic data we are able to determine how much solar power, visibility to Earth, and what the environment will be like. The interactive tool provides a 3D Interactive Lunar globe allowing the user to compare landing sites, see visibility over time, identify how much power they need, when they can communicate and plan rover routes. This project helps overcome the issue of finding areas that have consistent solar power and good communication for missions to the moon. Our interactive tool considers the true topography of an area, so we know how much sunlight and visibility we actually have, even though there are astronomical bodies above the horizon. Having considered these factors we hope to allow mission planners to make more informed decisions. This improves the reliability of missions, safety of surface operations and enables sustainable robotic and human exploration of the moon.
details:
Overview:

The Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive scientific and mission planning tool to find the most favorable landing sites and dates on the moon. We are focusing on the South pole of the moon due to the low sun angle and small changes in the terrain causing large differences in sunlight and communication with the earth. Rather than using a standard landing site map we use a combination of science data, astronomical data, terrain analysis and mission planning calculations to determine the optimal times to land at a site for sunlight, Earth visibility and good terrain conditions. The interactive 3D map of the moon allows you to search for your desired location, or look at existing landing sites. Multiple locations can be viewed and compared. A timeline has been included to show the environmental conditions for each location, and natural language queries can be used to adjust launch windows such as changing the launch window from March to June 2028. This will then adjust the rankings of the landing sites.

Functionality:

This application includes scientific data, astronomical calculations and a ranking engine.

Landing Site Terrain & Astronomy:

We used elevation data from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) using the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) to create the lunar terrain. From this the terrain horizons can be calculated.

The NAIF SPICE toolkit and JPL planetary ephemeris is used to calculate the position of the sun and earth in relation to the moon. The data is then converted to local coordinates for each landing site. The terrain horizons can be calculated and we determine if there are any obstructions to sunlight and earth visibility. The curvature of the moon and partial sun visibility of ~0.53 degrees is taken into consideration. This gives us a measure of not just if the sun is above the horizon, but how much of it can be seen from that location. Astronomy data is also calculated every 15 minutes from 2026 to 2030.

Landing Site Ranking:

We can rank landing sites based on several measurable factors:

- Amount of light received, maximum light or darkness periods.

- Sun height and percentage of sun visibility.

- Total Earth visibility and periods of both sunlight and earth visibility.

- Eclipse periods.

- Terrain height, slope and distance from geological faults.

- Distance from permanently shadowed areas.

- Estimated power requirements and battery size.

The south pole area is divided into a grid of around 1km and the ranking engine determines the best potential landing sites. An initial fast scan is performed and then details are calculated using high resolution terrain data for the top 50 landing sites in 15 minute time increments.

The whole moon can be searched using a grid of around 10km. The results will be clear to show they are low resolution.

The ranking engine can be used to rank sites based on goals and weighted sorting.

Mission Planner:

The results are displayed via several tools:

1. 3D interactive moon map with terrain, landing site markers, environmental data and terrain shadows.

2. Horizon plot for the surrounding terrain.

3. Shared timeline showing how much sunlight, earth visibility and communications will be available for 2-4 landing sites.

4. First person view to see what the terrain would look like from the landing site.

5. Ellipse analysis to give the best, average and worst environmental conditions from several sample points.

6. Power and battery tool to give an estimate of how much power will be available.

7. Communications tool to include Deep Space Network (DSN) visibility and link margin.

8. Rover Pathfinding tool using the A path finding algorithm to take terrain slope into consideration. It also takes into consideration periods where the rover will need to wait for sunlight.

9. Scenario comparison tool to see how changing the launch window will affect previous mission sites.

10. Results can be exported as CSV files and scenarios can be shared using links.

Benefits:

One of the biggest issues with exploring the moon is finding a landing site which is suitable. A site may look good from a geographical point of view but it may not be suitable. An example of this could be a site where there is a lot of sunlight throughout the lunar day but there are long periods of no sunlight. Or another site could have good sunlight conditions but not much earth visibility making communications difficult. This tool puts all the factors together into one platform. It makes complex science data easy to understand by providing interactive maps, timelines, comparisons and measurable mission variables. It can help users determine the best potential landing sites, what limitations may exist, what the best dates to go are, estimated power requirements and how to traverse the surface.

Impact:

Long term this will help make exploration of the moon safer, reliable and sustainable. This is especially useful for missions around the south pole due to the challenging conditions from sunlight, permanently shadowed areas and communications. The application provides an environment to analyze the terrain, perform astronomical calculations, plan power requirements and determine communications. This will help mission planners make more informed decisions. It also provides an educational tool for students, researchers and anyone interested in space exploration to look at real lunar environmental conditions. They will not have to process large amounts of science data themselves nor understand all the astronomical calculations.

Languages and Computational Tools:

Python – To collect and preprocess science data, generate astronomy data, process terrain data, validate and prepare data for the browser.

Rust – To create the calculation engine. Calculated terrain horizons, sunlight and earth visibility, environmental conditions, landing site ranking, power calculations, communications and rover path finding.

TypeScript – To create the interactive website.

JavaScript & React – To create the application.

WebAssembly (WASM) – Our calculation engine in rust can run in the browser.

External Tools and Libraries:

NASA LOLA – Elevation data for lunar surface.

NAIF SPICE & JPL DE440 – Astronomical data and coordinate conversion.

NumPy, SciPy & Rasterio – To perform scientific calculations.

PyO3 & wasm-bindgen – To allow the rust engine to work with Python and WASM.

CesiumJS – Interactive 3D moon map.

D3.js – To visualize science data.

Cloudflare Workers – Host for the application and natural language query.

OpenRouter – Natural language connection to a language model.

No bespoke hardware was required for this project. Everything is done in-browser using preprocessed science data.

Creativity & Considerations:

The main feature of this project is combining actual lunar terrain with astronomical calculations over time to determine the best landing sites. A basic version of this could be determining sunlight based on coordinates and the position of the sun. However this does not take into consideration the surrounding terrain. As the sun moves along the horizon at the lunar poles small hills or crater edges can cause obstruction meaning there is no sunlight even though the sun would technically be above the horizon. To overcome this we calculate the actual local terrain skyline and determine the amount of sunlight and earth visibility. We also take into consideration partial sun visibility and eclipse periods. Using natural language queries with a deterministic science engine is also very creative. Users can write sentences to change how their mission will be. An AI model translates this into adjustable search criteria. The science data and rankings are all calculated using our rust engine. This isn’t produced by AI and users can still use the traditional tools.

Considerations were made during development:

Scientific accuracy – Used known data from NASA, astronomical references and cross referenced.

Terrain – Taken into consideration with height, curvature, local horizons, slope, crater edges and permanently shadowed areas.

Lighting – Calculated how much sunlight, earth visibility and eclipse there will be over different mission dates.

Power – Calculated to determine if there will be constant sunlight, long periods of darkness and battery requirements.

Communications – Determined how much earth visibility and Deep Space Network opportunities there will be.

Mobility – Taken into consideration with slope and sunlight restrictions.

Speed – Large datasets were processed quickly with preprocessed data, spatial filtering, rust and WASM. Understandability – Complex science data made easy with interactive visuals, explanations and natural language queries. Science validation was also completed. We found a high correlation of 0.976 between the percentage sunlight we calculated and NASA’s Planetary Geodesy and Geophysics Data Archive (PGDA) average illumination values for 72,324 1km cells between 85°S and 90°S. We also found a high intersection over union of 0.81 between our permanently shadowed areas and the published reference mask. We also found 97.7% agreement between the cells. We also compared how much the sun would set at the location with the shutdown times reported by Chandrayaan-3 and Blue Ghost 1.

Overall we wanted to create more than a visualization tool. We wanted to create a science interactive tool which brings together real lunar geography, astronomy and mission planning.
